1.pericope_label: Nehemiah’s sad countenance before Artaxerxes, his request for Judah, and the letters granted

schools.summary: Henry will not let the four months’ delay look like idleness: Nehemiah did not sit still and say, Let God now do his own work, for I have no more to do, but set himself to forecast what he could do towards it, since our prayers must be seconded with our serious endeavours, else we mock God; he adds that the winter was no proper season for such a journey. On the fear he is specific, allowing that though Nehemiah was elsewhere a man of courage he was now sorely afraid, perhaps of the king’s wrath, those eastern monarchs assuming an absolute power of life and death, or else of misplacing a word and losing his request by mismanaging it — a humble self-diffidence being no man’s dispraise. He commends the meekness of the answer, made without reflection upon any man, and dwells on the fathers’ sepulchres: it is good for us to think often of them, since those who went before us in the world have also gone before us out of it, and all nations, even those with no expectation of the resurrection, have held them sacred and not to be violated. Of the prayer he observes that it was no solemn prayer but a secret sudden ejaculation, and that although Nehemiah had prayed solemnly for this very occasion he prays again when it comes to the push, ejaculations and solemn prayers not jostling out one another. On the queen he declines to settle whether she was his back friend, who would have hindered him, or his true friend, present to help the request forward, and takes the success to be owing not to merit, interest in the king, or good management, but to the good hand of his God upon him.

Gill offers the delay two ways, that Nehemiah either purposely spent the time in fasting and prayer on his people’s account, or that until now his turn did not come round to wait upon the king as cupbearer; he notes that it was still only the twentieth year of the reign because, while Nisan began the Jewish year, other nations dated their kings’ reigns from Tisri. On the king’s question he observes that Nehemiah had no disorder upon him to change his countenance, so that the sadness wanted explaining. He reports that some think the wish that the king live for ever was meant to take off any suspicion of a design upon his life, though it seems rather to have been a common salutation of the kings of those times. Of the forest he says it was the forest or mountain of Lebanon, which for its odoriferous and fruit-bearing trees was more like an orchard or paradise, that at the extreme part of it there was a city called Paradisus, and that such an officer was called among the Romans a Saltuarius. Of the queen he guesses Atossa the daughter of Cyrus, who might be the friendlier to the Jews on her father’s account, and observes that it was not common for the queens of Persia to dine with their husbands at all, finding the providence of God in her being present.

Clarke supplies a mechanism for the delay, supposing that the kings of Persia kept a different cup-bearer for each quarter of the year and that it had just now come to Nehemiah’s turn. He reads the king’s question as suspicion, as though Artaxerxes thought his servant harboured some bad design and saw conceived treachery or remorse in his face. On the salutation he insists Nehemiah wished his master no ill but long life and prosperity, and cites Aelian for the same form of words addressed to Artaxerxes Mnemon in connection with the annual offering of earth and water. The tombs of the dead, he says, were sacred among the ancients and nothing could appear more detestable than disturbing their remains, so that Nehemiah knew the circumstance would strongly interest the Persian king’s feelings. Before daring to prefer his request he made his prayer to God, and that by mental prayer, for to the spirit of prayer every place is a praying place. On the queen he denies she was a queen at all, taking shegal to mean rather a concubine or chief favourite, which the Septuagint renders as harlot, and denying that she was Esther; and on the grant he notices that Nehemiah might have pleaded long and faithful service but would not, attributing everything instead to the good hand of his God. Wesley agrees the delay was of four months and leaves the reason open, either that his turn of attending did not come till then or that till then he wanted a fit opportunity to move it. He explains the fear as arising both from the unusual and ungrateful thing of coming into the Persian king’s presence with any token of sorrow, and from the request being great and invidious and odious to most of the Persian courtiers, so that he feared a disappointment. He notes what the plea leaves out, that Nehemiah says not a word of the temple, speaking as he was before a heathen king who cared for none of these things, while the sepulchres are by all nations esteemed sacred and inviolable. Of the queen he marks her presence as unusual, the kings of Persia commonly dining alone, and supposes she expressed some kindness and promoted the request.

Ellicott attends to the dating, that Nisan is the old Abib, the first month of the Jewish year following the vernal equinox, and that since it is still the twentieth year of the king the beginning of his reign must be dated before Chisleu, the record adopting Persian dates so that the two months fall within one year. On the fear he locates the danger in court protocol: waiting on Providence, Nehemiah had discharged his duties for three months without being sad in the king’s presence, a sad countenance was never tolerated there, and though Artaxerxes was of a milder character than any other Persian monarch, the tone of his abrupt inquiry showed that in this respect he was no exception. He observes that Nehemiah does not yet betray the deepest desire of his heart but refers only to the desecration of his fathers’ sepulchres, an appeal which had great force with the Persians, who respected the tomb, and that his family was of Jerusalem. The ejaculatory prayer he marks as the first note of a habit characteristic of the whole book. Of the queen he proposes Damaspia, the one legitimate queen, and infers from her presence that this was no public feast, since at such a feast she would not have been there. Of the forest he makes Asaph a Jew and keeper of an artificial park or pleasure ground, the Persian pardes whence our Paradise, well planted with trees, the timber going to the gates of the fortress which protected the temple, to the city walls, and to Nehemiah’s own house, his appointment as governor being pre-supposed.

The courtiers, to whom the request would be invidious and odious; he feared a disappointment
The king’s wrath, those monarchs holding absolute power of life and death, or else misplacing a word

Alone in noticing that the plea says not one word of the temple, because it was made before a heathen king who cared for none of these things.
Alone in reckoning the regnal arithmetic from Persian dating, and alone in marking the ejaculatory prayer as the first instance of a habit running through the book.

9.pericope_label: The journey with the king’s escort, and the grief of Sanballat and Tobiah at his coming

schools.summary: Henry reads the captains of the army and the horsemen two ways at once, as a guard for Nehemiah and as a public honour, to show that he was a man whom the king did delight to honour, that all the king’s servants might respect him accordingly; those whom the King of kings sends, he adds, he thus protects and thus dignifies. On the enemies’ grief he supplies the motive: Sanballat and Tobiah, two of the Samaritans but by birth the one a Moabite and the other an Ammonite, were exceedingly grieved to see their paltry arts for weakening Israel baffled by a fair and generous project to strengthen them; and nothing is a greater vexation to the enemies of good people, who have misrepresented them to princes as turbulent and factious and not fit to live, than to see them stand right in the opinion of their rulers, their innocency cleared and their reproach rolled away, and to find them thought not merely fit to live but fit to be trusted.

Keil and Delitzsch set the escort beside a precedent, noting that Ezra had been ashamed to request a military escort of the Persian monarch, whereas the king gave to Nehemiah, as the high dignitary called Pecha, a guard of soldiers, and they judge that these certainly remained with him in Jerusalem also for his protection. On the enemies they reject the usual derivation of Sanballat’s title on a grammatical ground: he is certainly not from Horonaim in Moab, as older expositors imagined, since he would then have been called a Moabite, but from either the upper or the nether Beth-horon, formerly belonging to Ephraim and in Nehemiah’s time appertaining to the region of the Samaritans. Tobiah they take to be called the servant probably as being a servant or official of the Persian king, and both men to have been influential chiefs of the neighbouring hostile nations. They further notice that the grief is reported ironically, Nehemiah expressing himself from his enemies’ point of view when he says that a man was come to seek the welfare of the children of Israel. Ellicott follows them in placing Sanballat at one of the Beth-horons, which had been in Ephraim and were now in the kingdom of Samaria, and makes him satrap of Samaria under the Persians, whose secretary or minister was Tobiah the servant; he observes that Sanballat’s name is seemingly Babylonian while Tobiah’s is Hebrew, and puts the motive of the opposition in plain political terms, that the revival of Jerusalem would be a blow to the recent ascendency of Samaria.

Gill leaves the governors themselves unidentified, declining to say whether they were the same Tatnai and Shetharboznai who had held office in the second year of the king’s reign eighteen years before. Of Sanballat he says only that he either presided at Horonaim or sprang from thence, a city of Moab.

Clarke makes Sanballat probably a native of Horonaim, a Moabite by birth and at this time governor of the Samaritans under the king of Persia, and Tobiah an Ammonite and, under the Persian king, joint governor with Sanballat; he adds that some suppose this Sanballat to be the man who persuaded Alexander to build a temple on Mount Gerizim in favour of the Samaritans, while Pelagius thinks rather that there were two governors of the name. Wesley likewise derives the title from Horonaim, an eminent city of Moab, taking it for the place either of Sanballat’s birth or of his rule; but he reads Tobiah’s title as a record of origin rather than of office, so called probably from the condition out of which he had been advanced to his present power and dignity, which he offers as one reason why the man now carried himself so insolently, it being usual for persons suddenly raised from a low state so to demean themselves.

Certainly not Horonaim, since he would then be called a Moabite; from upper or nether Beth-horon, once of Ephraim and now Samaritan

debates.question: Why is Tobiah called the servant?

positions.view: Probably as a servant or official of the Persian king
As Sanballat’s own secretary or minister
As joint governor with Sanballat under the Persian king
From the low condition out of which he was raised, which accounts for his insolence

outliers.claim: Alone in contrasting the escort with Ezra, who had been ashamed to ask the king for one, and alone in reading the report of the enemies’ grief as spoken ironically from their own point of view.
Alone in canvassing whether this Sanballat is the man who later moved Alexander to build the temple on Gerizim, with Pelagius’s alternative of two governors of the name.

the king had sent captains of the army and horsemen with me

11.pericope_label: Three days’ rest, and the secret night ride round the broken walls and gates

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch have him rest three days as Ezra had also done, then rise in the night with a few men to ride round the wall and get a notion of its condition; the reason for taking but few, and those on foot, was that he had told no man what his God had put into his heart, for knowing the hostility of Sanballat and Tobiah he desired to keep his intention secret until an inspection had ascertained the magnitude and extent of the work and made him certain it could be carried into execution. On the route they place the valley-gate at or near the present Jaffa gate, leading to the valley of Gihon, and reckon the dragon-well, which occurs only here by that name, either identical with the well of Gihon, whose waters supply the upper and lower pools, or situated in its immediate neighbourhood; the fountain-gate they put on the eastern declivity of Zion but much farther south than the tradition that finds the ancient dung-gate elsewhere, in the neighbourhood of the pool of Siloah. The king’s pool they identify with what Josephus calls Solomon’s pool and places east of the spring of Siloah, which Robinson and Thenius take for the present Fountain of the Virgin, reporting that Bertheau rightly objects. The brook he ascended they take for the Kidron, and they correct older expositors who made him turn round and traverse the road by which he came, taking the word adverbially instead so that he simply came again into the valley-gate. On the silence they separate the titles, the nobles being heads of the different houses or races of the people and the rulers the authorities of the town, and explain that the builders are called the remnant by comparison with the priests, nobles and rulers. Ellicott makes the three days a time for rest and devotion after the example of Ezra, turns the valley-gate south so that it opens on Hinnom, and says the dragon-well is nowhere else mentioned and not now to be traced; the dung port he makes the way by which offal was taken to the valley of Hinnom, and the fountain-gate that of Siloah, called also the king’s pool. He reads the itineration as completing the circuit of the walls, takes the work as still to come, and justifies the caution of the procedure from subsequent events, since the city teemed with elements of danger while the nobles and rulers possessed no substantial repressive authority.

Gill has him resting from the fatigue of the journey and receiving the visits of his friends, as Ezra before him did, and explains that both the season of the night and the small number of men were chosen for greater secrecy, that the business might not yet be known and no schemes be formed to obstruct or discourage it. Of the valley-gate he notes that the gates had been burnt and not yet rebuilt, so that he went out where it formerly stood, and that it led, according to some, to the valley of Jehoshaphat, or rather to the valley of dead bodies through which the brook Kidron ran — the gate through which Christ went to Calvary, leading on to Shiloh, Bethhoron and Golan. The pool of the fountain he makes the way towards Siloah or Gihon and the road to the potter’s field, Bethlehem, Hebron, Gaza and Egypt, and he cites Rauwolff that the gate of the fountain was still standing outside the Tyropaeum valley which divides Zion from Moriah, so named because it led towards the fountain of Siloah, called the king’s pool. The brook he takes for Kidron. Of the rulers he observes that those who knew nothing of his errand seem to have been officers of the king of Persia, precisely because the next clause distinguishes them from the Jewish rulers.

Clarke declines the topography of the dragon well and explains its name instead, as perhaps taken from the representation of a dragon out of whose mouth the stream issued that proceeded from the well; the dung port he places on the eastern side of the city, the gate through which the filth of the city was carried into the valley of Hinnom. The gate of the fountain he makes that of Siloah, and the king’s pool not a pool at all but probably the aqueduct made by Hezekiah to bring the waters of Gihon to the city of David. Of the secrecy he says Nehemiah made no person privy to his design, that he might hide everything as much as possible from their enemies until he had all things in readiness, lest they should take measures to defeat the work. Wesley explains the choice of night as concealing his intentions as long as he could, knowing that the life of his business lay in secrecy and expedition, and the single beast as a means to prevent noise; the footmen who accompanied him he takes to have directed and led him in the way, his design being to go round the city and observe the compass and condition of the walls and gates, that he might make sufficient provision for the work. Where the beast could not pass he says simply that the way was obstructed with heaps of rubbish, and he glosses those that did the work as those who were to do it, whom Nehemiah intended to employ.

Henry finds in the silence a motive the others do not supply, that Nehemiah did not tell them at first what he came about because he would not seem to do it for ostentation, and because, if he found the thing impracticable, he might retreat the more honourably — upright humble men will not sound a trumpet before their alms or any other of their good offices. He notes too that while the great men of the city took little notice of him, he took great notice of them and their state, rising in the night to view the ruins probably by moonlight, that he might see what was to be done and in what method they must go about it, whether the old foundation would serve and what of the old materials would be of use. From this he draws three rules: that good work is likely to be well done when it is first well considered; that it is the wisdom of those engaged in public business to see with their own eyes rather than proceed on the reports of others, yet to do it without noise and if possible unobserved; and that those who would build up the church’s walls must first take notice of the ruins of them, since those who would know how to amend must enquire what is amiss, what needs reformation, and what may serve as it is.

17.pericope_label: The call to build and the people’s assent, met by the scorn of Sanballat, Tobiah and Geshem

schools.summary: Henry presses the manner of the appeal: Nehemiah did not undertake the work without them, for it could not be the work of one man, nor did he charge or command imperiously though he had the king’s commission, but in a friendly brotherly way exhorted and excited them to join him. He notes that Nehemiah took no praise to himself, as though the design were a good thought of his own, but acknowledged that God had put it into his heart, and that he produced the king’s commission to show how readily it was granted, so that both he and they might be encouraged in an undertaking God had smiled upon. On the answer he draws the lesson that they had all seen the desolations of Jerusalem and none of them had proposed the repair, but when one man proposed it they all consented: many a good work would find hands enough to be laid to it if there were but one good head to lead in it, and it is a pity a good motion should be lost purely for want of someone to move it and to break the ice. By stirring up ourselves and one another to that which is good, he adds, we strengthen ourselves and one another, the great reason why we are weak in our duty being that we are cold to it, indifferent and unresolved. Of the adversaries he observes that they represented the undertaking both as a silly thing, laughing at builders who could not finish what they began, and as a wicked thing, no better than treason, keeping up the old invidious charge of rebellion though the builders now had the king’s commission and his protection; and that the Jews slighted these discouragements with reason, bearing themselves up with this, that they were the servants of the God of heaven and were acting for him. In his closing application he turns it on the reader: the enmity of the serpent’s seed against the cause of Christ is confined to no age or nation, the church of God asks for our help, and we should not let business, pleasure or the support of a party so engage our attention that Zion and her welfare shall be nothing to us.

Keil and Delitzsch read the two things Nehemiah produced as calculated to gain the favourable regard of the assembly for his design, namely the hand which his God had graciously provided for him, that is, the gracious ordering of his journey to Jerusalem, and the king’s words spoken with respect to the building of the wall, of which the narrative had so far reported only the order given to the keeper of the royal forest; encouraged by this information, the assembly exclaimed that they would rise up and build. Of the adversaries they add Geshem the Arabian, whose fuller pronunciation Gashmu occurs later in the book, and take him for the chief of some Arab race dwelling in South Palestine not far from Jerusalem. The irony of the charge they locate precisely: the enemies did not give the Jews credit for power to build fortifications, so as to be able to rebel at all, and Sanballat afterwards reproaches them with rebellion again in an open letter. Of the reply they note its impressive gravity and explain the last term, that only members of the congregation, who may hope to live on in their descendants in Jerusalem, can be said to have a memorial there. Ellicott observes that the opening word carries no note of time, and has Nehemiah wait until his plans were matured before making an earnest appeal to their patriotism, relating his providential call together with the king’s commission so that the people were thoroughly enlisted in the good cause. Geshem he makes the third of a triumvirate, and denies that any of them were independent chieftains, Tobiah being Sanballat’s servant and counsellor and Geshem probably the leader of an Arabian company mostly in his service; the account of their contemptuous opposition he finds given in a few touches, as is the contempt with which it was met. The reply he calls a defiance in the name of the God of heaven, and reads the closing words as implying that, as in the days of Zerubbabel, the Samaritan enemies really desired a share in the undertaking, Nehemiah giving Zerubbabel’s answer but strengthening it, so that they had nothing in common with Jerusalem, not even a place in its memorials save one of shame.

Gill itemises the providence Nehemiah told them of: the kind providence of God in exalting him in the court of the king of Persia, in giving him an opportunity of laying the sad case of Jerusalem before him, and in inclining the king’s heart to show him favour and grant his request; and he identifies those addressed as the priests and princes of the Jews. Of Geshem he allows that this third man might be both an Arabian by birth and governor of some part of Arabia near Judea. Of the reply he notes that Nehemiah answered with much spirit and boldness, not at all intimidated by their scoffs or threats.

Clarke says briefly that Nehemiah opened to them his design and his commission, and makes Geshem some chief of the Arabs contiguous to Samaria who had joined with Sanballat and Tobiah to distress the Jews and hinder their work. The charge of rebellion he reads as a calculated manoeuvre, said in order to raise jealousies in the king’s mind and induce him to recall his ordinance. On the reply he recalls that to be a citizen of Jerusalem was a high honour, and that they would not permit those who did not belong to the tribes of Israel to dwell there, Zerubbabel having given the Samaritans the same answer. Wesley hears resolution in the people’s words themselves, that they would do it with vigour and diligence and resolution, as those determined to go through with it, and takes the strengthened hands to be their own and one another’s. He divides the reply, no portion meaning that the adversaries had no authority over the Jews nor interest in their church and state but were aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and no memorial meaning no testimony or monument either of their relation by birth or religion, or of any kindness done to the people or to the place.

Alone in locating the irony of the taunt in the enemies’ low estimate of Jewish capacity to fortify at all, and alone in reporting Gashmu as the fuller form of the name.
